text: How The Patch Works What the problem was: The issue was that the INIC3639 (I assume) was initially designed not for ODDs but for SSDs - to be used in applications like M.2 or MSATA enclosures. Because of this this oversight and the fact that the programmers at Initio needed to be able to flash firmware to the USB to SATA converter, they hijacked the 0x3B (WRITE BUFFER) and 0x3C (READ BUFFER) SCSI opcodes completely. The problem with this, is that these opcodes are critical to flashing the ODD, and thus completely hijacking them breaks functionality. Based on testing, I am also highly certain that Libredrive also uses these opcodes for loading the temporary patch that allows it to function. How It works now: Instead of unconditionally diverting these commands to the bridge IC, as bridge-local vendor commands, the INIC3639 now forwards all commands other than 0x3C mode 0x01 (used to read the bridge’s 64-byte identity/configuration window) and 0x3B mode 0x10 (used to access the MPTool vendor channel) to the SATA interface which allows the MPTool to continue functioning properly and flashing and Libredrive to work correctly. How it was implemented: This was done by placing a 50 byte dispatcher in unused 0xFF padding.

text: Can you provide a source regarding "LG" withdrawing from the Blu-ray drive market? I suspect you've confused LG (which manufactured Blu-ray players for TVs, until pulling out of the market in 2024 December) with Hitachi-LG Data Storage (a joint venture between Hitachi and LG, which manufactures optical drives for PCs, that carry "LG" branding). In my searches for tech news articles, I found plenty of articles discussing LG's withdrawal from the Blu-ray player market, and plenty of articles regarding Pioneer withdrawing from the PC optical drive market, but none of these articles mentioned HL-DT-ST. LG's withdrawal from the Blu-ray player market had no impact on HL-DT-ST. HL-DT-ST USB drives are still available at every retailer I checked. Several 3rd-party OEMs are also still selling optical drives based on HL-DT-ST's BU40N chipset (which is considered the best chipset HL-DT-ST has ever manufactured), such as the Verbatim 43888, and the ThinkPenguin TPE-BLUDVUSB3. Note that I can't find HL-DT-ST's 5.25 inch drives at any retailer. In one case, the retailer lists the BH16NS55 as "End of Life", and doesn't list any other 5.25 inch drives. I assume that HL-DT-ST has stopped manufacturing 5.25 inch drives, which isn't surprising, given that their 5.25 inch drives had a reputation on these forums for being vastly inferior to their USB drives. In my personal experience, the BH16NS55 regularly returns garbled data during prolonged or high-speed use, and often scratches Blu-ray discs in the process. With Pioneer no longer manufacturing optical drives, there's simply no reason why anyone should still go out of their way to build a desktop PC with 5.25 inch bays (PC cases with 5.25 inch bays are becoming increasingly rare and expensive), as opposed to just buying USB optical drives.
label: question
